en: In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*, it is stated that attaining the principle is even more luminous than this. To eliminate the ten non-virtues of body, speech, and mind is called "contact.

To purify the three karmas and attain right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) means that eliminating the ten non-virtues so that the continuity of life is [righteous] is called "attaining the contact of right livelihood. This is termed "reception" (*vedanā*).
Regarding "appropriation" (*parigraha*):
when sentient beings experience [an object], they grasp at the presence or absence of suffering within that objective sphere;
this is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Because the wisdom of the second stage is more luminous than before and it experiences the merits of the second stage, feeling is termed "appropriation."
Because of sensation (*vedanā*), afflictions arise.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can embrace [the cessation of] the retribution of the three evil realms;
therefore, sensation is taken as the means of inclusion.
This is a designation established based on what has been eliminated.
Contemplation is the mind of the third stage;
it exhausts all coarse and subtle afflictions pertaining to the truths to be seen.
The mind of understanding surpasses the previous two stages and is termed "increased attainment.
This is the mind of the fourth stage, which destroys the afflictions through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
One is able to destroy the superior-grade afflictions within the path of cultivation by relying upon the merit of right mindfulness as the leader; that is, taking mindfulness as the sovereign.
The following passage uses worldly analogies to explain this.
For one who has entered meditative concentration,

the mind of the five stages cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; because it can skillfully discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and induce the subsequent wisdom,
it takes the primary [factors] as its guide.
Regarding these thirty-seven factors:
in the sixth stage, one contemplates emptiness through prajñā;
in the seventh stage, one possesses the prajñā capable of discerning the characteristics of phenomena.
Wisdom and understanding are supreme;
it is through wisdom that one attains supremacy.
If one destroys the afflictions and departs from the three kinds of [obstructions], one will attain the meritorious virtues.
In the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages,
the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of these three stages is termed "reality" (*bhūta*).
Although one may attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa and liberation through these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, [it is only here that they are truly realized].
From the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat,
these four fruits are still not called ultimate;
they merely involve the severance of the practices associated with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The cessation of the sphere of mental activity is called Great Nirvana.
Furthermore, from here on, the fourth section provides an understanding based on the characteristics of cause and effect.
That which is the mind of affectionate longing is "desire."
The thought of desiring to attain bodhi and the thought of desiring to give birth to the second stage are called "desire" (chanda).
Taking this inferior-grade affectionate thought as the cause for the arising of superior-grade [wholesome states] is called "contact" (sparśa).
This is what is meant by "cause."
The first two minds give rise to the second stage, which is termed "reception" (*parigraha*) because it involves grasping [the teachings].
Regarding "due to relying on a virtuous friend":
because of the preceding two stages, one’s contemplation of the constant principle and understanding of the principle become increasingly clear; this is termed "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
Regarding these four dharmas:

by relying on the preceding faculties as causes and conditions, one is able to cultivate and grow the four dharmas of the four stages; that which is called "mindfulness" (smṛti) is the uncontaminated (anāsrava) wisdom of the five stages, while those of the sixth and seventh stages are termed "sovereign excellence."
Regarding these three factors as causes:
by means of the wisdom of the master, one gives rise to the latter three stages, which are called the two liberations.
Ignorance (*moha*) is able to obstruct wisdom, and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to bind the mind.
By severing craving, the mind attains liberation;
by removing delusion, wisdom attains clarity.
This twofold liberation of mind and wisdom is what is called reality.
When these eight dharmas are continuously realized through the emptiness of their characteristics and one ultimately attains the fruit, it is called Great Nirvana.
"Desire" refers to that which follows the initial arousal of the mind.
This fifth section concerns the profound and shallow understandings within the dharma of renunciation.
The initial mind of the lower grade of the first stage is called the "first outflow-free [attainment]" and is named the "initial departure from the household life.
As for "contact" (*sparśa*) being the "fourfold formal act" (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*):
this "contact" refers to the higher grade of mind, which is like the fourfold formal act performed after having departed from the household life; it is named the mind of the second stage.
This encompasses the arising of two kinds of precepts following the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of fourfold proclamation).
"Increasing" means becoming superior, just as one cultivates and attains the four dhyāna-concentrations based upon the two kinds of precepts.
"The master’s turning [of power] becomes stronger" is like the arising of wisdom after meditative concentration, which severs the fetters of the vision of the truths until they are exhausted.
During the path of cultivation, one exhausts six grades of fetters and realizes the two fruits of Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin;
the Guide exhausts the three subtle delusions.
This is similar to the stage of an Anāgāmin.
As for "superior," there are two kinds of *prajñā*; that which is superior is named Arhat.
As for "real," it refers to the final three stages where the true mind’s flow of dharmas simultaneously illuminates both existence and non-existence; being most sharp, it is named Pratyekabuddha.
"Ultimate" (*atyanta*) carries the sense of reaching fulfillment through causes; it is named the unsurpassed great fruit (*anuttara-phala*).
As for "desire" (*chanda*) being termed "cognition" (*vijñāna*):
among the nine factors, desire is foremost as the very beginning.
Just as within a single retribution, consciousness is the very first, it is said that "desire" is named after consciousness.
As for "contact" being named after the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), this refers to the fundamental contact that confronts the six objects;
just as when one is on the first stage, the mind of superior grade contacts the second stage, so too does contact arise with respect to its objects to produce understanding.
Therefore, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are called "contact" (sparśa).

As for what is termed "appropriation" (upādāna), it is called "appropriation" because its essence consists of receiving and experiencing pleasure and pain; since it is capable of appropriating the two lower levels of merit, it is said that appropriation is what receives.
Regarding the designation "ignorance" (*avidyā*):
among the delusions produced by past ignorance, this is predominant.
It is like the superior grade of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) within the three stages of faith (*śraddhā*), which is stronger than what preceded it and thus receives its name.
Regarding the statement that "name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the master":

because name and form serve as mutual supports, they prevent [the continuity] from being destroyed or dispersed, allowing it to continue and receive a single segment of karmic retribution for a hundred years.
Just as the four elements are the basis for the subsequent succession of the untainted mind, it is said that name-and-form is the master.
That which guides is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving is fundamentally the defiled attachment to objects;
it is like the mind of the fifth stage (*pañcamī-bhūmi*) which is able to induce the subsequent wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, it is said that "guidance" is a name for craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
As for "superiority" being grasping (*upādāna*):
to be stained by and grasp at objects is called grasping.
Just as the wisdom of *prajñā* in the sixth stage and the wisdom of *upāya* in the seventh stage—
these two types of wisdom are called "superior" because their realization of principle is even more luminous.
Regarding "existence by way of actual designation":
that which contains the fruit but has not yet emitted it is called existence;
within the analysis of birth and aging, it is forcefully designated as existence.

To clarify that the minds of these three stages— the eighth, ninth, and tenth bhūmis— are the Great Non-arising Patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and because their merit surpasses [that of the preceding stages],
their great fruit is clearly distinguished and their significance is powerful,
it is said that they are "truly named existent."
Ultimate [reality] is called old age and death.
Old age and death are fundamentally the final stage of a single karmic retribution,
just as the fruit of nirvana is the ultimate destination.
Therefore, it is said that "ultimate" refers to old age and death;
this is because the preceding twelve factors attain what is like nirvana through the attainment of the preceding eight factors.
From the words "Kāśyapa said," the fourth section briefly condenses the aforementioned nine factors into three factors.
Among these, there are also six banners that clarify the meaning.
First, the names are listed in direct succession.
Second, from "The faculties are precisely the 'having acted'" (*kṛta*) onwards, the names are translated and their meanings explained.
The third section, beginning with "In the future world," directly explains the two dharmas of the present and the immediate.
The fourth section, beginning with "The faculty is that which seeks," correctly names the three dharmas.
The fifth section, beginning with "The faculty is the path of vision," addresses the meaning of awakening, non-awakening, and clarity.
From "The sixth faculty is the direct cause" onwards, the meaning of the arising of understanding through the characteristics of cause and effect is addressed.
From "How does the fundamental cause increase and take on difference?
onwards, the answer is given by the phrase "Good son."
From the first stage to the seventh stage, all are the initial arousal [of the mind].
As for the cause, the final three stages are called "similar" because they remain together within the state of the flow of the Dharma and are not interrupted by other characteristics.
The "increasing" refers to the three [aspects] tending toward cessation; the "similar" refers to the attainment of the fruit; and the "true similar" refers to future retribution.
Because it has not yet been experienced in the present, it is categorized as a cause belonging to the practitioner.
When the myriad practices are complete and the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) manifests, it is called "increase.
The subsequent text is easy to understand.
Kāśyapa asked: "If nirvāṇa is thus, how can it be attained?"
This is the reason for the inquiry.

It was stated above that within the state of mind of the "ground-nature" (bhūmi-prakṛti), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ) are still not taken up as the holy life (brahmacarya).
It is only when one reaches from the first ground (prathamā bhūmiḥ) upward until Buddhahood, and the empty mind continues in succession, that one is able to practice the holy life.
When people hear this, they give rise to the thought of regressing.
Only from the first bhūmi upward can one be considered to have entered the holy life (brahmacarya);
those below that level do not yet attain it.
Today, among our assembly, there is no cause for that which lies beneath the earth.
How, then, can the practice upon the earth serve as a stepping stone? Since both cause and practice are not yet established, [how can we attain the fruit?]
"How can the fruit of Great Nirvana be attained?
The passage beginning with "Good son" answers this:
the fourfold assembly merely cultivates the ten signs as the cause.
In the next life, upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one will ultimately attain Great Nirvāṇa through the continuity [of practice].
You shall obtain it simply by cultivating the ten signs;
why wait for many further practices?
This is its "wisdom that is remote" (jñāna-dūra).
It is named according to its arising from characteristics (nimitta).
The meaning of the ten characteristics is easy to understand from the text.
Regarding the *Kauṇḍinyavarga*, the masters of the sūtra explain that while the preceding two chapters exhorted people to practice the Path,
once the practice of the Path is complete, one attains the fruit.
Therefore, the *Kauṇḍinya-varga* is established with the intent that its meaning be propagated;
thus, Kauṇḍinya is first addressed because it is intended to clarify that he is the foremost elder among the assembly.
Desiring that [the teaching] circulate for a thousand years without perishing after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he gave his command for two reasons:
first, because of his singular intention;
second, because the discourse on the sūtra was concluded, and the conditions for the ten ṛṣis’ realization of the Way lay with Cunda.
It is because of two intentions that he is called "Life.
Thirdly, at the beginning of his arrival, when he attained the Way in the Deer Park and first preached the Four Noble Truths, he was for Ājñātakauṇḍinya;
today, as he delivers his final teaching at the Twin Śāla Trees, he is likewise for Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
This indicates that the Tathāgata has a beginning and an end.
Within this context, the circulation [of the Dharma] results in attaining eternal form through impermanent form;
since it is called "circulation," [it implies such a process].
Regarding the profound meaning of the superior grade,
why is it called "circulation"?
The Tathāgata himself said:
I have previously stated that form is impermanent.
You shall extinguish impermanent form and attain permanent form.
In the future, you shall propagate this Dharma of mine.
Therefore, this chapter is circulated under this title.
"Form" (rūpa) is the substance of the eternal fruit;
by severing birth and death, one reaches the exhaustion of attachment to form.
Its essence is clear, luminous, and manifest; its meaning is identical to that of form (*rūpa*).
The Tathāgata has severed the three lower types of sensation (*vedanā*), which have forever vanished;
its essence is the ultimate.
The reception of true merit is called "feeling" (vedanā).
The wisdom of true illumination that penetrates to the exhaustion of conventional names and marks is called "perception" (saṃjñā).
For the practitioner, the accumulation of birth and death within the lower stages is termed "volitional formations" (saṃskāra).
The Tathāgata’s severing of all evils and the accumulation of myriad virtues is called "conduct" (*caryā*).
The consciousness of the lower stages that discriminates blue and yellow is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
The true wisdom that penetrates the ultimate reality is called "consciousness."
The "aggregates" (skandha) of the lower realms are the "coverings" (āvaraṇa).
Because practitioners constantly dwell within birth and death, they are called the "fruit of the aggregates.

That which manifests the aggregates is so named because it can cover and obscure the practitioner, preventing them from being carefree and beyond the mundane world. Thus, they are called "aggregates."
If there is anyone who can understand the meaning of the aforementioned permanence and impermanence, they are called a śramaṇa;
one who has truly stilled evil is called a brāhmaṇa, a true practitioner of purity.
Within my Buddha-dharma, there are such śramaṇas.
If, apart from the Buddha-dharma, there were the dharma of a śramaṇa or a person who is a śramaṇa, such a thing is impossible.
Those who claim to have the Way are all merely followers of external paths (tīrthikas). Why is this?
The purpose of composing this work is to critique the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who seek to establish a self-soul (ātman),
and to debate with them regarding the Buddha’s teachings in order to distinguish right from wrong.
Therefore, this text was composed to bring such discourse back to its correct transformation.
Various non-Buddhists say:
"Gautama previously taught that suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self [are the truth]."
I have assembled my disciples;
therefore, you may endure it,
for you are different from me in your understanding.
Those without wisdom follow him;
those with wisdom return to me.
Therefore, it is said that [the former] may be endured.
Today, while he was preaching permanence, bliss, self, and purity within the Śāla Grove,
all his disciples have been converted and brought to submission;
I cannot bear this in my heart.
Therefore, he sought out those who would debate and censure him. Among the assembly was a brahmin;
the Tathāgata ascended to the sixteenth heavenly realm to debate the principles of the Dharma with various non-Buddhist practitioners.
All have been completely transformed through the True Teaching.
Within this group, there is another segment of ten seers who are non-Buddhists;
they are now about to come forward to debate the doctrine.
Among these ten sages, it is essential that those with the sharpest faculties possess the capacity for swift awakening.
